subject: pharmacology
title: Cytotoxic Anticancer VIII: Cell Cycle Specificity, Combination Logic and Tumour Lysis Syndrome

steps.tx: **Cell cycle specificity** sorts cytotoxics by the phase they kill in: antimetabolites in S, vinca and taxanes in M, etoposide in late S and G2, bleomycin in G2 and M, against cell cycle non specific alkylators and platinums that damage DNA in any phase including resting cells. Phase specific drugs kill a fraction per exposure and reward schedule (prolonged or repeated dosing catches more cells entering the phase), while non specific agents show linear dose kill.
steps.say: Phase drugs need time and repetition; non specific drugs need dose. Schedule follows the sort.

left.title: Phase specific
points: Late S G2: etoposide; G2 M: bleomycin
Log kill per exposure capped: schedule dependent

steps.tx: A cytotoxic kills cells that are in its phase and spares the rest until they arrive. Antimetabolites sit on the S arc, vinca alkaloids and taxanes on M, and etoposide on late S and G2. Alkylators and platinum drugs sit off the wheel, because they damage DNA in every phase, including rest. A **phase-specific** drug needs a timetable that meets cells as they enter the sensitive arc. One large dose misses every cell that was elsewhere.
steps.say: Antimetabolites act in S phase, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase, and etoposide in late S and G2. Alkylators and platinum drugs act in any phase. Phase-specific drugs are scheduled so more cells are caught in the sensitive phase.

vis.alt: Cell-cycle wheel with anticancer drugs marked on the G1, S, G2 and M arcs.
vis.caption: The cycle is drawn as a wheel, with antimetabolites on S, vinca alkaloids and taxanes on M, and bleomycin and etoposide toward G2. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Log kill** mathematics governs expectations: a given therapy kills a constant fraction (say 99 percent, two logs) not a constant number, so a tumour of 10 to the 12 cells needs repeated cycles interleaved with regrowth, adjuvant therapy exists to kill micrometastatic fractions while they are small, and cure requires the last clonogenic cell, which immune surveillance and luck finish in the classic model. Gompertzian growth (small tumours grow fastest fractionally) explains adjuvant advantage.
steps.say: Chemotherapy kills fractions, not numbers; small residual disease is where cure is won.

nodes.label: Repeated cycles ratchet the fraction down
Adjuvant therapy erases micrometastases at smallest size

steps.tx: **Combination chemotherapy** obeys four design rules written by the successful regimens of earlier lessons: each drug active alone, mechanisms distinct (non cross resistant), toxicities non overlapping where possible (vincristine's marrow sparing beside cyclophosphamide), and schedules that keep dose intensity. Dose reductions and delays surrender the arithmetic, which is why growth factors and antiemetic prophylaxis are efficacy drugs in disguise.
steps.say: Active alone, different mechanism, different toxicity, full dose on time: the four rules behind every acronym.

left.title: Design rules
points: Dose intensity defended by supportive care

right.title: Failure modes
points: Two marrow drugs without growth factor plan
Cross resistant partners repeating one mechanism

steps.tx: **Tumour lysis syndrome** is successful kill outrunning excretion: bulky chemosensitive disease (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, high LDH solid tumours) releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids converted to uric acid, causing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia with hypocalcaemia, uric acid nephropathy and acute kidney injury, largely within days of first therapy. Risk stratification before cycle one assigns hydration intensity and hypouricaemic strategy.
steps.say: Killing a kilogram of lymphoma releases its insides at once; kidneys meet the flood first.

left.title: Laboratory TLS
points: LDH marks tumour bulk and turnover

steps.tx: **Tumour lysis syndrome** is successful killing that outruns excretion. Bulky chemosensitive disease, including Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, and some solid tumours with a high LDH, releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that are converted to uric acid. The clinical picture is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia with hypocalcaemia, uric acid nephropathy, and acute kidney injury, largely within days of the first therapy. Risk is stratified before cycle one. That stratum decides how intensive hydration should be and which strategy will lower uric acid.
steps.say: Rapid destruction of bulky Burkitt lymphoma or acute lymphoblastic leukaemia releases potassium, phosphate, and uric acid at once. Within days the kidneys meet hyperkalaemia, high phosphate with low calcium, and uric acid nephropathy. Risk is scored before the first cycle so fluids and uric acid control match the load.

vis.alt: A flowchart shows lysed tumour cells releasing potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that become uric acid and injure the kidney.
vis.caption: Cell breakdown feeds hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia with a fall in calcium, and uric acid nephropathy within days of the first treatment. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Allopurinol** prevents new uric acid formation (xanthine oxidase blockade from the gout lesson) and suits low and intermediate risk with vigorous hydration, started before chemotherapy, while **rasburicase** (recombinant urate oxidase) destroys existing uric acid within hours for high risk or established lysis, fenced by G6PD deficiency (hydrogen peroxide haemolysis) and by blood samples that keep degrading uric acid in the tube unless chilled. Urinary alkalinisation has retired beside rasburicase era evidence.
steps.say: Allopurinol stops uric acid being made; rasburicase eats what already exists. Risk chooses.

right.title: Rasburicase lane
points: Samples on ice: ex vivo degradation falsifies levels

steps.tx: **TLS management** beyond hypouricaemics is electrolyte triage: hyperkalaemia treated by the hyperkalaemia ladder (calcium, insulin dextrose, potassium binders, dialysis thresholds), phosphate binders and avoidance of calcium unless symptomatic hypocalcaemia (calcium phosphate precipitation), generous hydration titrated to urine output, and nephrology engaged early because dialysis in TLS treats a moving metabolic target.
steps.say: Treat potassium, bind phosphate, spare calcium unless symptoms; dialysis thresholds come early in TLS.

nodes.label: Electrolytes and urine output every 4 to 6 hours
Phosphate binders, calcium only if symptomatic
Dialysis for refractory potassium, phosphate or fluid

steps.tx: **Sanctuary sites** explain intrathecal therapy and testicular vigilance: the blood brain and blood testis barriers exclude most cytotoxics, so ALL protocols deliver methotrexate and cytarabine intrathecally and high dose systemic methotrexate crosses by gradient, while drugs that penetrate (temozolomide, nitrosoureas, procarbazine) anchor brain tumour regimens. Relapse in sanctuaries after systemic cure is barrier pharmacology announcing itself.
steps.say: Barriers create sanctuaries; protocols invade them deliberately or relapse moves in.

left.title: Barrier problem
points: High dose methotrexate crosses by gradient

right.title: Barrier penetrators
points: Radiation reserved by age and relapse rules

steps.tx: **Response language** completes cytotoxic literacy: complete and partial response by RECIST measurements, progression dates that trigger regimen change, performance status gating eligibility, and adjuvant, neoadjuvant, concurrent and palliative intents that decide how much toxicity arithmetic is rational. The same drug is four different prescriptions under four intents, which is why intent is documented before dose.
steps.say: Intent writes the toxicity budget; RECIST writes the report card. Both precede cycle two.
